subject: PHS
vignette: A biostatistician reviews the design of a trial of a new oral anticoagulant. She notes that the probability of a type II error (beta) for the planned analysis is 0.20.
question: Which of the following best describes the statistical power of this trial?

options.text: 0.20, the probability that the study will fail to detect a true effect
The probability of making a type I error, conventionally 0.05
0.80, the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false
0.95, the probability that the confidence interval excludes the null value
The probability that the null hypothesis is true

explanation_correct: Statistical power is 1 - beta, the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false—that is, the probability of correctly detecting a real effect or difference. With beta = 0.20, power = 1 - 0.20 = 0.80, which is the conventional target for trial design. Power is improved by increasing sample size, expected effect size, precision of measurement, and the alpha level.

explanation_incorrect.A: 0.20 is beta, the probability of a type II (false-negative) error, which is the complement of power, not power itself.
explanation_incorrect.B: The probability of a type I error is alpha, not power; power concerns failing to reject a false null hypothesis.
explanation_incorrect.D: 1 - alpha = 0.95 corresponds to the confidence level of a 95% confidence interval, a separate concept from power.
explanation_incorrect.E: Power is defined only in terms of the behavior of the test when the null hypothesis is false; it says nothing about whether the null hypothesis is true.

educationalObjective: Statistical power = 1 - beta, the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false, with 80% a common design target.

subject: PHS
vignette: A pilot study of a new diuretic for heart failure fails to detect a benefit on hospitalization rates, and the principal investigator is told that the study was underpowered. She asks her team which design change would most improve the study's ability to detect a real effect in the definitive trial.
question: Which of the following changes would most directly increase the statistical power of the definitive trial?

options.text: Decreasing the expected effect size of the intervention
Lowering the alpha level from 0.05 to 0.01
Decreasing the precision of the outcome measurement
Increasing the tolerated probability of a type II error
Increasing the sample size of enrolled participants

explanation_correct: Power increases with larger sample size—'there is power in numbers'—as well as with a larger expected effect size, greater precision of measurement, and a higher alpha level. Enrolling more participants reduces the standard error, making a true difference easier to detect and decreasing beta (the type II error rate).

explanation_incorrect.A: A smaller expected effect size is harder to detect, so power decreases rather than increases.
explanation_incorrect.B: Lowering alpha makes the significance threshold more stringent, which decreases power; raising alpha would increase it.
explanation_incorrect.C: Less precise measurements add noise to the data, making true differences harder to detect and lowering power.
explanation_incorrect.D: Accepting a higher probability of a type II error is the same as accepting lower power (power = 1 - beta).

educationalObjective: Power rises with increased sample size, larger expected effect size, greater precision of measurement, and a higher alpha level.

subject: PHS
vignette: A biostatistics consultant is asked to review a completed study of a new smoking-cessation program before publication. She determines that the study had a 20% probability of committing a type II error.
question: What is the probability that this study correctly rejected the null hypothesis when it was false?

options.text: It cannot be determined without knowing the sample size

explanation_correct: The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis is the statistical power, which equals 1 - beta. With a 20% probability of a type II error (beta = 0.20), power = 1 - 0.20 = 0.80, or 80%. This means that if the smoking-cessation program truly works, the study had an 80% chance of demonstrating a statistically significant difference.

explanation_incorrect.B: 20% is beta, the probability of a type II error (failing to detect a real effect), not the probability of correctly detecting one.
explanation_incorrect.C: 95% is 1 - alpha, the confidence level corresponding to a 95% confidence interval, not statistical power.
explanation_incorrect.D: 5% is the conventional alpha level, the tolerated probability of a type I error.
explanation_incorrect.E: Power is fully determined by beta, which was given directly; sample size is only one of the factors that influences beta.

educationalObjective: Statistical power = 1 - beta and represents the probability of rejecting the null hypothesis when it is false.

subject: PHS
vignette: A small pilot trial enrolls 25 patients per arm and finds no significant difference between a new neuropathic pain drug and placebo (p = 0.30). The drug is actually effective, and the investigators plan a follow-up study.
question: Which of the following modifications would most likely help the follow-up study avoid the same false-negative conclusion?

options.text: Repeat the study with the same methods but half as many participants per group
Lower the significance threshold to alpha = 0.01 to reduce the risk of a false positive
Use a less precise instrument to measure pain so that the outcome variability increases
Recruit substantially more participants to increase the probability of detecting a true difference
Assume a smaller expected treatment effect in the sample size calculation

explanation_correct: A p value of 0.30 in a tiny trial with a truly effective drug is the classic picture of a type II (false-negative) error caused by inadequate sample size. Because power increases with increased sample size ('there is power in numbers'), recruiting more participants is the most direct fix: it lowers the standard error and raises the probability of rejecting a false null hypothesis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Halving the sample size further decreases power and makes a false-negative result even more likely.
explanation_incorrect.B: Tightening alpha from 0.05 to 0.01 makes rejection of H0 harder, decreasing power and increasing the type II error rate.
explanation_incorrect.C: Increasing outcome variability (lower measurement precision) reduces power, since noisier data obscure real differences.
explanation_incorrect.E: Planning around a smaller effect size makes the study less able to detect the (real, but modest) treatment effect; power increases with larger expected effect size.

educationalObjective: Increasing sample size increases power and is the primary safeguard against type II (false-negative) errors in underpowered trials.
